lesson.title: The Vowel Bridges
lesson.subtitle: ice → ijs, house → huis, book → boek — the real Dutch work

hook.title: The Consonants Are Free; the Vowels Are the Work
hook.content: The consonant twins give you the word; the vowels give you the Dutch pronunciation. IJ is /ɛi/, UI is /œy/, OE is /u/. English ice, house and book are the spelling keys.

pattern.title: Three spelling bridges
pattern.content: English i/y often answers to Dutch ij: ijs, wijn, vijf. English ou/ow often answers to Dutch ui: huis, muis. English oo often answers to Dutch oe: boek, voet, goed. These are spelling bridges, not claims that the vowels sound identical.
pattern.linguist_note: The Dutch digraphs ij and ui are old spellings for diphthongs; oe spells a long /u/. English orthography preserves different vowels from the same Germanic stock.
pattern.trap_note: Dutch oe is /u/, while English 'book' has /ʊ/. Do not copy the English vowel; read the Dutch spelling and use the Dutch sound.

exercises.prompt: Match each English meaning with its Dutch twin (The Vowel Bridges):
exercises.target_answer: het ijs, het huis, het boek, de wijn, vijf, de muis
exercises.meaning: ice, house, book, wine, five, mouse
exercises.explanation: These are the anchors of "The Vowel Bridges": read each Dutch form through the pattern, not as a new word.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence says: “The ice is cold.”?
exercises.explanation: “Het ijs is koud.” is the Dutch form; the other readings bend the pattern of “The Vowel Bridges”.

cues: It means: My house is small.
exercises.explanation: “Mijn huis is klein.” puts the thought together the Dutch way — Three spelling bridges.

diagnosis.slip: an English-shaped word order slipped in
diagnosis.cue: Dutch oe is /u/, while English 'book' has /ʊ/. Do not copy the English vowel; read the Dutch spelling and use the Dutch sound.

exercises.prompt: Which English sentence is built the Dutch way?
exercises.explanation: “Het boek is goed.” is word-for-word “The book is good.”. The odd English is the lesson — never a model to produce. Pattern: Three spelling bridges.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
cues: It means: The wine is red.
exercises.explanation: “De wijn is rood.” reuses only material taught in “The Vowel Bridges” — Three spelling bridges.
exercises.affirmation: You heard “De wijn is rood.” — a sentence built from the lesson's own Dutch, practising Three spelling bridges.

twist.prompt: One more, no safety net — say: “The mouse is small.”
twist.explanation: Muis is the ui twin of mouse; the sentence reuses the adjective frame.

summary.outcome: Read ij, ui and oe as Dutch vowel signals and match them to English spelling twins.
summary.takeaway: Vowels are where the course earns its keep; consonants are the free part.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on De Brug: IJ / UI / OE Gym.

ijs.etymology_derivation: English ice and Dutch ijs are the same word.

huis.etymology_derivation: English house and Dutch huis are the same word; ui answers to ou.

boek.etymology_derivation: English book and Dutch boek share the spelling bridge; Dutch oe is /u/.

wijn.etymology_derivation: Latin vīnum gave English wine and Dutch wijn.

vijf.etymology_derivation: English five and Dutch vijf are the same word.

muis.etymology_derivation: English mouse and Dutch muis are the same word.

vowel_ij.name: The IJ Bridge
vowel_ij.phonetic_rule: Dutch ij is /ɛi/ and often answers to English i/y: ice → ijs, wine → wijn, five → vijf.
vowel_ij.historical_linguistics: The digraph ij spells a Dutch diphthong; English orthography kept a different vowel from the same Germanic stock.
vowel_ij.philological_note: IJ is two letters but one sound. It is not English /aɪ/.
